rv.q: This is innovative theatre, shining with intelligence, which brings richness to our cultural tussle with the problem of ancient statues and their rightful place in the world.
It’s a hard thing to pin down, other than to say that it really is way too long, and succeeds in its restless breadth where it doesn’t in giving us depth.
This highly entertaining political satire of topical issues encourages us to care about and applaud those fighting for the return of objects Britain has stolen from other countries.
This is still a fine and important contribution to a growing debate, and not one confined to museology.
It is exactly the kind of play you want the Royal Court to present in this space.
The writing is insightful and concise, rendering many scenes simultaneously touching, shocking and funny.

cn.t: Joel Tan's ambitious play about cultural repatriation earns praise for its inventive structure and theatrical ingenuity, with critics applauding its playful, unconventional approach to exploring the return of artifacts through distinct, interconnected scenes.
